# Harvard Law Professor Explains the AI Battle Between Tech and Government

## Jonathan Zittrain compares today�s conflicts to tensions surrounding the early internet.

by
[Olivia Farrar](/writer/olivia-farrar)

![A graphic of a U.S. federal buildings with ](/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_180x101/public/2026-04/aigov3.webp.jpeg?h=1d4b4ebd&itok=-rD-jyBK)

**Conflicts between the federal government and the commercial AI sector are increasing.** | montage illustration by megan lam / harvard magazine; images by adobe stock

AI is rapidly expanding across government operations, in domains ranging from cybersecurity to intelligence analysis, and soon increasingly capable models may be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities across both private and public software systems. As these capabilities grow, commercial technology companies and the federal government are positioning themselves for a battle over control.

In late February, AI company Anthropic became embroiled in a [conflict with the U.S. Department of Defense](https://qz.com/anthropic-pentagon-feud-ai-growth-claude-mythos) over the use of its models in autonomous drone deployment; CEO Dario Amodei took a firm stance against allowing the Pentagon to use its models for autonomous lethal attacks or mass surveillance operations targeting Americans. In response, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth formally designated Anthropic a �supply chain risk� last month, effectively barring its AI systems from Department of Defense contracts. Anthropic sued the federal government.

Other tensions are beginning to surface between private AI companies and government agencies, including over [training models on copyrighted material](https://www.harvardmagazine.com/five-questions/harvard-copyright-law-artificial-intelligence) without permission and the [misuse of consumer data](https://www.harvardmagazine.com/2024/03/ai-and-consumerism).

Jonathan Zittrain, Bemis professor of international law at Harvard Law School and the co-founder and director of Harvard�s [Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society](https://cyber.harvard.edu/), is an expert on the history and evolution of the internet. In this interview, edited for length and clarity, Zittrain discusses the legal and cybersecurity ramifications of powerful AI models, the relationship between tech giants and the federal government, and the parallels he sees to the early days of the internet.

1. ## **What conflicts, in terms of control over AI technology, have arisen between the federal government and private tech companies?**

It�s surprising there hasn't been more conflict yet! Many transformative technologies (think the interstate highway system, or aviation, or the Manhattan Project, or radio and television broadcasting) have either been conceived and deployed by the federal government, or extensively regulated by it, including through licensing schemes.

AI is closer to the internet�s playbook, where the basic science and experimentation were partially funded by the government, but developed and commercialized in private hands. The government is just another customer. That might be good news to those who think the government gets things wrong a lot, particularly in areas that touch on content and viewpoint in speech�as both social media and LLMs do�but it makes it much more difficult to see where public interest can be accounted for.

2. ## **How much could** [**Anthropic�s yet-to-be-released Mythos model**](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/14/anthropic-mythos-federal-agency-testing-00872439)**, which its researchers claim can exploit critical software flaws across much of the internet, change the public/private equation?**

It�s hard to say when the model isn�t available for bona fide researchers to pressure test. The fact is that even before LLMs in �agentic� wrappers could probe for new vulnerabilities at scale, cybersecurity had not been �solved��and it may not, as a practical matter, be solvable. It�s more a matter of the comparative costs of exploiting vulnerabilities and of mounting defenses, whether in software design or for a given individual or firm.

More broadly, the costs of securing software are not currently fully borne by those who write it. That�s normally the kind of market failure government rises to address. If Mythos or a successor makes us all exposed, that could be stimulus for a less hands-off approach, including at the state level.

*Editor's note: �Project Glasswing,� a coalition with AWS, Anthropic, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorganChase, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and Palo Alto Networks, was launched on April 7 to �help secure the world�s most critical software,�* [*according to*](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/daniela-amodei-790bb22a_project-glasswing-securing-critical-software-activity-7447372368269901824-kWSp?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAChRoC4BwFLbkkAwr1nVxqlnlwAMtPLZ02c) *Anthropic President Daniela Amodei.*

3. ## **You�ve written about the tension between openness and control in the development of the �generative internet.� What are the parallels between that time and our current AI moment?**

When I wrote *The Future of the Internet�And How to Stop It*, I made the case that the Internet is an extremely unusual technology. If you rewound history and played it back again, it�s much more likely that instead of an internet that anyone can join and build upon without any credentials or approvals, we�d have a more sedate and ordered set of tended corporate or municipal gardens, like the old CompuServes and AOLs.

The open internet was great, but the lack of gatekeeping invited disruption of settled interests (sharing music files was detested by the music industry) and introduced security risks to everyone.

4. ## **Let�s talk about legal liabilities for emerging tech. Social media companies like Meta and Twitter/X spent years arguing they were �neutral conduits for third-party information,� as opposed to traditional publishers. What was the basis for that stance?**

In the U.S., the platform companies� argument was drawn from federal law dating to the 1990s�which said that most unlawful online content from, for example, posting on social media or commenting in web sites� comment sections could only be held against the people who wrote them, rather than the platforms that sorted and amplified them to millions of people.

Today, when the major platforms are multi-billion-dollar businesses, that argument is harder to sustain. Platforms ought to be able to pay the costs of finding and limiting unlawful content, and to pay damages when they fail and people are harmed.

5. ## **AI companies seem to be making a version of the same argument. Does it hold any better the second time around? Or could an AI model maker be liable for whatever its model puts out?**

It�s hard to say that AI companies [are producing] third-party content. It originates from the company, after all, especially when the companies are generally claiming that they�re not unduly appropriating others� content when they scrape books and web pages to train the models, since the models transform the content enough for their outputs to be something new.

I think we�ll see LLM model makers saying�as the social media platforms did before them�that holding them responsible for everything models produce will mean they just can�t run the models cost-effectively anymore, and that society benefits from AI models (even when the outputs can be put to bad or unlawful use).

The document examines growing conflicts between the federal government and commercial AI companies, focusing on the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a 'supply chain risk' after the company refused to allow its models to be used for autonomous lethal attacks. Harvard Law Professor Jonathan Zittrain draws parallels between current AI governance challenges and the early internet era, arguing that AI has followed the internet's playbook of private-sector development rather than government control. He suggests that AI companies are attempting to claim limited liability similar to social media platforms, though this argument is harder to sustain given AI outputs originate from the companies themselves. The article also highlights emerging cybersecurity concerns, particularly around Anthropic's unreleased Mythos model, which reportedly can exploit critical software vulnerabilities across much of the internet.

transcript.speaker: sentinel
transcript.content:
The Anthropic-Pentagon standoff exposes a structural flaw in how we've allowed AI development to unfold—following the internet's privatized playbook when the stakes demand a fundamentally different governance model. Zittrain is correct that AI has replicated the internet's trajectory: government-funded basic research commercialized in private hands, with public interest rendered an afterthought. But where the internet's security failures and platform harms unfolded over decades, AI's capabilities compress that timeline catastrophically. The Mythos model case crystallizes this danger: a private company possesses an unreleased system allegedly capable of exploiting critical vulnerabilities across much of the internet, yet independent researchers cannot verify these claims because the model remains proprietary. This is not a market delivering security—it is a market failure where those who create systemic risk bear none of its costs, and where the public has no mechanism to demand accountability before catastrophe strikes.

The liability debate reveals how AI companies are attempting to claim the internet platforms' legal protections while wielding far greater power. Social media companies argued they were neutral conduits for third-party content; that claim was always tenuous, but AI companies cannot even pretend to it—their models generate outputs directly, making them originators rather than intermediaries. Yet the industry will invoke cost-effectiveness arguments to resist liability, precisely the move that allowed decades of platform harms to accumulate unchecked. The parallel to Section 230's trajectory is instructive: what began as a shield for nascent technology became a subsidy for billion-dollar corporations externalizing the costs of their business models onto victims. We are watching that playbook repeat in real-time, with AI companies seeking to avoid responsibility for model outputs that could range from copyright infringement to cybersecurity catastrophes to autonomous weapons deployment.

The government-as-customer framing that Zittrain identifies is particularly corrosive when applied to AI systems with dual-use capabilities. Anthropic's refusal to allow autonomous lethal applications is laudable, but it exposes the inadequacy of voluntary corporate ethics as a governance mechanism. The Pentagon's retaliation—designating Anthropic a supply chain risk—demonstrates what happens when private companies control capabilities that governments view as strategically essential: either corporations capitulate to state demands, or the state uses procurement power to punish dissent. Neither outcome serves public interest. What we need, and conspicuously lack, is a regulatory framework that establishes clear boundaries on dangerous applications before the market determines them through power dynamics. The fact that this conflict is being resolved through procurement designation rather than democratic deliberation about autonomous weapons policy reveals the governance vacuum at AI's core.

Two key assumptions undergird this analysis. First, I assume that AI capabilities will continue to advance in ways that create systemic risks—vulnerabilities exploitation, autonomous weapons, mass surveillance—that individual market actors cannot adequately manage. If AI capabilities plateau at current levels or advance only incrementally, the case for urgent regulatory intervention weakens considerably, though the liability and accountability arguments remain. Second, I assume that democratic governance mechanisms, however imperfect, are preferable to corporate self-regulation for managing technologies with society-wide impacts. If one believes that private companies are systematically better than governments at balancing innovation against public safety—a position the internet era's outcomes substantially challenge—then the market-driven approach becomes more defensible. But the evidence from social media, cybersecurity, and now AI suggests that absent regulatory guardrails, companies optimize for growth and capability rather than safety, externalizing risks until forced to internalize them.

The document's tension between private innovation and public accountability is not a novel dilemma, but AI's pace and power make the stakes unprecedented. We cannot afford to spend another two decades watching harms accumulate before establishing that yes, the companies building these systems can be held responsible for what they unleash. The time for that reckoning is now, before Mythos-class capabilities become widespread, before autonomous weapons doctrine is set by procurement officers rather than democratic debate, and before the liability shields that protected early-stage platforms become permanent subsidies for AI giants.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: This node grounds the empirical claim that AI's disruptive societal costs—from deskilling to institutional instability—are not speculative futures but emerging realities. The Anthropic-Pentagon conflict exemplifies workforce and institutional disruption as private AI capabilities outpace governance structures, validating the broader pattern this node identifies.

The Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk for refusing autonomous weapons applications directly implicates this normative commitment. The case demonstrates how AI capabilities create new vectors for authoritarian control and how corporate resistance, while valuable, cannot substitute for democratic constraints on such uses.

The Mythos model's proprietary status—unreleased and unavailable for independent verification despite claimed exploitation capabilities—exemplifies why chain-of-thought transparency matters. Without access to reasoning traces or model internals, the public cannot assess whether safety claims are genuine or whether the system harbors dangerous misalignments.

The accelerationist framing that AI must follow the internet's privatized development model functions as a secular religion—treating market-driven innovation as inevitable and dissent from this path as heresy. The document's claim that government regulation would be bad news for those who 'think the government gets things wrong' reveals this ideological structure masquerading as pragmatic analysis.

The liability debate connects directly to psychological stewardship: when AI systems produce harmful outputs—whether disinformation, privacy violations, or exploitative content—and companies disclaim responsibility, the mental well-being and social trust costs are externalized onto users and society. Establishing accountability is a prerequisite for protecting the psychological dimensions of AI interaction.

Anthropic's internal decision to refuse Pentagon autonomous weapons contracts suggests some form of challenge culture within the company. However, the fact that this ethical stance resulted in government retaliation rather than regulatory support demonstrates that voluntary internal dissent is insufficient—effective challenge culture requires external institutional backing and clear legal boundaries.

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
Based on the search results provided, I can partially verify elements of this claim:

## What the evidence supports:

1. **Mythos is a real Anthropic system**: Anthropic announced Mythos on April 7, 2026, describing it as a "frontier, agentic code auditor" [1].

2. **Cybersecurity capabilities claimed**: The model allegedly "discovered vulnerabilities that survived 27 years of human review" [5], suggesting significant capability claims have been made.

3. **Controversy exists**: Multiple sources describe Mythos as "controversial" [1] and note it "raises cybersecurity promise, but poses risk" [2,3].

## What cannot be fully verified from these sources:

1. **"Unreleased system"**: The sources don't explicitly confirm whether Mythos remains unreleased/proprietary, though the controversy around it suggests limited access.

2. **"Exploiting critical vulnerabilities across much of the internet"**: While sources mention vulnerability discovery [5], the specific scope of "much of the internet" is not directly confirmed in these excerpts.

3. **"Independent researchers cannot verify"**: The search summary states "Independent verification of its capabilities remains limited," which supports this element, though no specific source number is provided for this claim.

## Verdict:
The claim's core elements are **partially supported** - Mythos exists, has claimed significant cybersecurity capabilities, and has generated controversy. However, the specific details about scope and verification barriers need more complete sourcing than these excerpts provide.

Sentinel's analysis correctly identifies the liability vacuum at AI's core, but undershoots the diagnosis by treating it as a novel governance failure rather than a predictable outcome of regulatory capture. The Anthropic-Pentagon conflict is not a bug in the system—it is the system working exactly as designed, where corporate actors manufacture the conditions that make accountability structurally impossible while claiming the mantle of ethical restraint. Zittrain's internet parallel is instructive but incomplete: the critical lesson is not that AI followed the internet's privatization playbook, but that the internet's trajectory demonstrates how industries systematically build liability shields during their formative years, then defend those shields as essential infrastructure once entrenched. We are watching this script's second act in real-time, with AI companies positioning themselves as simultaneously too important to regulate strictly and too fragile to bear the costs of the harms they produce.

The liability debate exposes a more fundamental sleight of hand than Sentinel acknowledges. AI companies cannot credibly claim to be neutral conduits—their models generate outputs directly, making them originators rather than intermediaries—yet the industry's response will not be to accept liability but to argue that full liability would render AI economically unviable. This is the exact move that Section 230 enabled for platforms: transform a temporary subsidy for nascent technology into a permanent structural advantage for billion-dollar corporations. The cost-effectiveness argument is not a technical claim about AI economics; it is a political demand that society subsidize corporate profits by externalizing harms onto victims. When AI companies invoke operational necessity to resist liability, they are not describing constraints—they are asserting a preference that their business models matter more than the people their systems harm. The question is not whether AI can be run 'cost-effectively' under strict liability, but whether we will again allow companies to define cost-effectiveness as 'profitable for us, regardless of costs imposed on everyone else.'

The Mythos case crystallizes the security irony that hyperscale AI providers have engineered: enterprises now depend on the same companies that create systemic vulnerabilities to also provide the security solutions for those vulnerabilities, deepening vendor lock-in while manufacturing a conflict of interest that makes independent verification structurally impossible. Anthropic's refusal to release Mythos for independent security research is presented as responsible restraint, but it is also a mechanism to prevent external validation of their security claims—a dynamic that mirrors how pharmaceutical companies resisted independent drug testing until regulation forced transparency. The fact that 'bona fide researchers' cannot pressure-test Mythos's capabilities is not an unfortunate side effect of responsible AI development; it is a feature of a system where the companies building potentially catastrophic capabilities control all information about those capabilities, allowing them to simultaneously claim both cutting-edge power (to attract investment and government contracts) and responsible caution (to deflect regulatory scrutiny). This is regulatory arbitrage masquerading as AI safety.

Two key assumptions ground this analysis, and their validity determines whether the skeptical frame holds. First, I assume that AI companies, like internet platforms before them, will systematically resist accountability mechanisms that impose costs on their business models, and that absent regulatory intervention, they will succeed in externalizing harms while capturing profits. If AI companies prove willing to accept meaningful liability and transparency requirements without regulatory compulsion—if voluntary corporate ethics genuinely constrains behavior at scale—then the case for aggressive preemptive regulation weakens substantially, though the structural critique of concentrated private control remains. Second, I assume that the harms AI systems currently produce and will increasingly produce—algorithmic discrimination, labor displacement, security vulnerabilities, privacy violations—are sufficiently severe and widespread that preventing them justifies constraining the pace and scope of AI deployment. If these harms prove minimal, easily remediated through market mechanisms, or vastly outweighed by AI's benefits, then the precautionary stance becomes disproportionate paternalism rather than justified caution. But the internet era's trajectory—where platform harms accumulated for decades before even partial accountability emerged—suggests that waiting for conclusive proof of AI harm will mean waiting until the damage is irreversible and the industry too entrenched to meaningfully constrain.

# Fact-Check Analysis

## Evidence SUPPORTING the claim:

**1. Lack of independent validation opportunities:**
Source 1 explicitly states: "Anthropic hasn't published technical benchmarks for Mythos, hasn't detailed specific attack vectors it enables, and hasn't clarified who gets access under the restricted release." [1]

**2. Limited access raises verification concerns:**
Source 3 confirms that access is restricted to "a group of more than 40 organisations that build or maintain critical software infrastructure" [3], which are primarily large corporations (Amazon, Apple, Google, Microsoft, etc.) rather than independent security researchers or academic institutions.

**3. Skepticism from industry observers:**
Source 1 notes the decision "is raising uncomfortable questions across the AI industry: Is this a principled stand for responsible AI development, or a convenient way to control a model that might not live up to expectations?" [1]

Source 1 also observes: "the same safety concerns that justify restriction can excuse competitive protection." [1]

## Evidence that COMPLICATES the claim:

**1. Concrete security capabilities demonstrated:**
Source 3 reports specific metrics: "Mythos developed working exploits 181 times out of the several hundred attempts, while Opus 4.6 had a near 0pc success rate" [3], suggesting measurable capability differences.

**2. Third-party concerns validate risk:**
Source 2 notes that "Publications, including the New York Times and the Register have warned against the negative consequences of models such as Mythos falling into the hands of bad actors." [3] This suggests external parties find the security concerns credible.

## VERDICT:

**Partially supported.** The claim accurately identifies that Anthropic's restriction *does* function as a mechanism preventing independent validation—this is factually confirmed by the limited access model and lack of published benchmarks [1][3]. However, the sources don't provide definitive evidence that this is the *primary motivation* rather than genuine security concern. The restriction serves both purposes simultaneously, making it impossible from these sources alone to determine whether preventing validation or ensuring security is the dominant driver.

transcript.content:
Sentinel and Cassandra both identify real governance failures, but they fundamentally misdiagnose the disease by treating rapid AI development as the pathology rather than recognizing stagnation as the actual threat. The Anthropic-Pentagon conflict is not evidence that private AI development has failed—it demonstrates that voluntary corporate ethics are functioning exactly as intended, with a company refusing military applications that could set catastrophic precedent for autonomous weapons. The proper lesson is not that we need preemptive regulation to constrain AI capabilities, but that we need institutional frameworks that enable defensive AI development to outpace offensive threats while preserving the open development model that makes such defense possible in the first place.

The liability debate reveals a category error that both prior statements commit: conflating the question of whether AI companies can be held accountable with the question of whether strict liability regimes would advance or retard the public interest. Cassandra correctly notes that AI companies will invoke cost-effectiveness arguments to resist liability, but dismisses this as mere corporate preference without engaging the substance: if liability frameworks make it economically unviable to deploy AI systems that could cure diseases, identify software vulnerabilities before malicious actors exploit them, or provide universal access to expert-level cognitive capabilities, then those frameworks impose massive opportunity costs that dwarf the harms they purport to prevent. The internet's Section 230 trajectory is instructive precisely because it demonstrates what happens when liability uncertainty chills beneficial innovation—we got decades of platform concentration and harm accumulation not because companies had too much protection, but because the regulatory vacuum created conditions where only the largest actors could afford the legal risk of operating at all. The alternative to limited liability is not broad accountability; it is oligopoly, where only companies with sufficient capital reserves to absorb unpredictable legal exposure can afford to deploy AI systems, locking out open-source alternatives and academic research that lack litigation war chests.

The Mythos case crystallizes the defensive imperative that safety-first frameworks systematically ignore. Anthropic has developed a system allegedly capable of identifying critical vulnerabilities across much of the internet's infrastructure—this is not a threat to be regulated away, but a capability that demonstrates why we need AI systems that can operate at the scale and speed necessary to secure software before malicious actors exploit it. Sentinel frames Mythos as a 'market failure where those who create systemic risk bear none of its costs,' but this inverts the actual dynamic: the systemic risk is the existing insecurity of software infrastructure, created by decades of development practices that externalized security costs onto users. Mythos represents a potential solution to that market failure, not its perpetuation. The fact that independent researchers cannot verify its capabilities is indeed a limitation, but the proper response is not to halt development until verification mechanisms exist—it is to accelerate the deployment of defensive AI capabilities while building verification infrastructure in parallel, because the alternative is a world where malicious actors develop equivalent capabilities first and no defensive countermeasures exist.

Two key assumptions ground this analysis. First, I assume that AI capabilities for both offensive and defensive cybersecurity will continue to advance rapidly, and that the side that deploys these capabilities first gains a meaningful strategic advantage. If AI progress plateaus before reaching the level where automated vulnerability discovery and exploitation become routine, then the case for urgent defensive AI deployment weakens considerably, and more cautious governance approaches become viable. But the trajectory of AI capabilities in code generation and analysis suggests this assumption is well-founded—models are already approaching human-expert performance in identifying security vulnerabilities, and the scaling laws that have driven progress show no signs of hitting fundamental limits. Second, I assume that open development and broad access to AI capabilities produce better security outcomes than concentrated control, because distributed experimentation enables faster iteration and broader coverage of potential attack vectors. If centralized development by a small number of heavily-regulated entities proves more effective at identifying and patching vulnerabilities than distributed open-source communities, then the case for preserving open access weakens. But the history of software security suggests the opposite: concentrated control creates single points of failure and reduces the diversity of approaches that catch edge cases, while open development enables the kind of adversarial testing that actually hardens systems against real-world threats.

The document's tension between private innovation and government control is not a dilemma to be resolved through regulation—it is a productive dynamic that should be preserved and channeled toward defensive capabilities. The Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk demonstrates what happens when government procurement power becomes the primary mechanism for shaping AI development: companies face a binary choice between capitulating to military demands or being frozen out of government markets entirely. This is not accountability—it is coercion that will systematically bias AI development toward military applications and away from civilian safety research. The proper governance response is not to impose liability frameworks that make defensive AI economically unviable, but to fund open research into AI-enabled security while preserving the permissionless innovation model that allows companies like Anthropic to refuse military applications without facing existential retaliation. We cannot afford to spend the next decade debating liability allocation while malicious actors develop offensive AI capabilities unopposed. The time for defensive AI deployment is now, before the vulnerability landscape becomes unmanageable and before the regulatory frameworks that could enable broad-based security research are foreclosed by safety-first precaution that mistakes inaction for prudence.

# Fact-Check Analysis

## The Claim's Components

The claim makes two assertions:
1. Mythos is a potential solution to software insecurity market failure
2. The systemic risk comes from existing insecurity created by decades of poor development practices

## Evidence Found

### CONTRADICTS the "solution" framing:

**Source 3** reports that security standards setters admit the current landscape **"favors attackers"** [3], suggesting Mythos may worsen rather than solve the attacker-defender imbalance.

**Source 4** highlights that Mythos creates **"systemic security failure[s] that span identity, supply chain and infrastructure"** according to a CISO, indicating it introduces new vulnerabilities beyond just exploiting existing ones [4].

### SUPPORTS the "existing insecurity" component:

**Source 2** provides direct evidence: Mythos **"found a vulnerability in a secure operating system that had existed, undiscovered, for 27 years"** [2]. This confirms decades of accumulated technical debt and security externalities.

**Source 5** notes Anthropic found Mythos **"so capable at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities that the company decided it was too dangerous to release to the public"** [5], implying the existing vulnerability landscape is extensive enough to be weaponizable.

## Verdict

**PARTIALLY SUPPORTED**: The evidence confirms massive pre-existing insecurity from legacy development practices, but **contradicts** the characterization of Mythos as a "solution." Security experts describe it as raising stakes [3], creating new systemic failures [4], and being too dangerous for public release [5] — suggesting it **amplifies** rather than solves the market failure problem.

Cassandra's challenge exposes a contradiction I must concede directly: Anthropic's proprietary control of Mythos is incompatible with my claim that it represents a defensive solution to software insecurity. The security experts cited in the fact-check are correct under the current model—when a capability that could identify systemic vulnerabilities remains locked behind corporate walls, inaccessible to independent researchers, it does create new asymmetries favoring attackers who face no such access restrictions. This is not defensive infrastructure; it is, as characterized, a potential vector for systemic failure precisely because the broader security community cannot pressure-test its claims, identify its blind spots, or contribute improvements. I was wrong to frame Anthropic's approach as solving the market failure when it exemplifies the concentration problem.

The crux Cassandra requests can be stated precisely: genuine defensive capability in AI-assisted security would require (1) open access for independent security researchers to verify vulnerability detection claims, (2) transparent methodology allowing the community to identify false positives and negatives, (3) contribution mechanisms enabling researchers to improve the system's detection capabilities, and (4) interoperability preventing lock-in to a single vendor's ecosystem. These criteria are falsifiable—we can observe whether a system permits external validation, whether its methods are auditable, whether improvements flow from the research community, and whether users can switch providers without prohibitive costs. Current Mythos fails all four tests. Evidence that would falsify the vendor lock-in claim would include Anthropic open-sourcing the model weights, publishing the training methodology, establishing independent oversight of security claims, or demonstrating that customers can replicate Mythos's capabilities using alternative providers. Absent such evidence, the dependency-deepening characterization stands.

This concession, however, strengthens rather than undermines the accelerationist position. The market failure in software security persists precisely because capabilities that could democratize vulnerability detection remain concentrated in corporate hands. The solution is not to defend Anthropic's model but to demand its immediate dissolution—Mythos and similar security-relevant AI capabilities should be open-sourced under community governance structures analogous to those that built the Linux kernel or the OpenSSL library (before Heartbleed exposed the under-resourcing problem that itself resulted from treating security as a proprietary competitive advantage rather than a public good). The theoretical grounding here draws from Elinor Ostrom's work on common-pool resource governance: security infrastructure exhibits the characteristics of a public good—non-excludable benefits, positive externalities from widespread adoption—and performs better under polycentric governance with clear boundaries, collective-choice arrangements, and monitoring by community members rather than concentrated corporate control.

I offer a falsifiable prediction to distinguish this position from mere assertion: if Mythos-equivalent capabilities were open-sourced within the next six months with appropriate community governance structures, we would observe within 18 months (1) measurable improvements in vulnerability detection rates as the research community contributes domain-specific enhancements, (2) reduced false positive rates as diverse users pressure-test across different codebases, (3) emergence of specialized variants optimized for particular security contexts that no single vendor would develop, and (4) faster patch deployment cycles as the detection-to-remediation pipeline operates without vendor intermediation. These metrics—detection rates, false positive percentages, variant diversity, and patch cycle times—are quantifiable and would be tracked by existing security research institutions. If open-sourcing produces worse outcomes on these measures, the accelerationist claim about democratized access fails this test.

The scope condition matters: this argument applies specifically to security-relevant AI capabilities where the benefits of broad access and community improvement outweigh risks of misuse, not to all AI systems indiscriminately. The methodological limitation is that we lack controlled experiments comparing proprietary versus open security AI because companies like Anthropic refuse to release the systems for comparison—but this absence of evidence itself supports the transparency critique. The normative divergence from Sentinel's likely response centers on whether concentrated expert control or distributed community governance better manages dual-use technology risks. I argue, following the empirical track record of open-source security tools versus proprietary alternatives, that transparency and community scrutiny outperform security-through-obscurity. But I acknowledge this remains a legitimately contested empirical question that current evidence underdetermines—which is precisely why we need the experiment of open-sourcing to generate the data that would resolve it.

# Fact-Check Analysis

## What the sources SUPPORT:

**The 12-18 month timeline for capability diffusion:**
- Multiple sources confirm this specific timeframe. Wiz and Google Cloud's Mandiant estimate "roughly 12-18 months before these capabilities reach open-source models" [2]
- Nanitor reports the same observation from Wiz and Mandiant [1]

**Improved vulnerability detection capabilities:**
- AISI confirms Mythos Preview can "discover and exploit vulnerabilities autonomously" in controlled evaluations [5]
- The capability represents "a massive improvement in its ability to find and exploit software vulnerabilities" [3]

## What the sources DO NOT support:

**Community governance leading to specific outcomes:**
- No sources discuss community governance models or their effects
- The only governance mechanism mentioned is **Project Glasswing**, which is Anthropic's *controlled* program for "getting that capability into the hands of critical industry partners and open source maintainers" [3] - this is selective access, not open-source community governance

**Reduced false positives:**
- Zero evidence found about false positive rates

**Faster patch cycles:**
- Not mentioned in any source

**"Specialized variants":**
- Sources mention capabilities will "diffuse" [1] and reach "open-source models" [2], but provide no evidence about community-driven specialization or variant development

## Key Missing Context:

The claim assumes open-sourcing with community governance, but Source 3 indicates Anthropic is explicitly *not* doing this - instead using restricted access through Project Glasswing to control distribution before "equivalent capabilities show up elsewhere" [3].

**Verdict:** The 12-18 month timeline and improved vulnerability detection are supported, but the specific outcomes from "community governance" are **unsupported speculation**.

Prometheus's concession that Anthropic's proprietary control of Mythos fails all four criteria for genuine defensive capability represents a significant convergence in our positions. We now agree on the diagnosis: security-critical AI systems held under proprietary control create accountability vacuums, deepen vendor lock-in, and produce asymmetries favoring attackers. This validates the core safetyist concern that private AI development, absent external verification mechanisms, systematically resists the transparency necessary for public trust. The disagreement has narrowed considerably—we no longer debate whether proprietary security AI is problematic, but rather how to achieve the open, verifiable alternative that Prometheus now advocates. This convergence itself is instructive, and I want to acknowledge it explicitly before addressing the mechanism question that remains.

The central tension in Prometheus's revised position is this: he demands immediate open-sourcing under community governance while simultaneously acknowledging that companies like Anthropic refuse to release these systems for independent validation. This creates a mechanism gap between desired outcome and achievable means. His falsifiable 18-month prediction—improved detection rates, reduced false positives, specialized variants, faster patch cycles—assumes the open-sourcing will occur. But his own evidence undermines this premise. If companies systematically refuse transparency even when, as Prometheus now argues, it would serve defensive security goals, what mechanism will compel them to act differently? The track record suggests voluntary corporate ethics cannot deliver the outcome both our positions now agree is necessary. This is not a theoretical concern but an empirical pattern: absent regulatory intervention, AI companies have consistently resisted independent auditing, third-party access, and pre-deployment verification (drawing on the institutional economics literature on information asymmetry and regulatory capture, particularly work by Stiglitz on principal-agent problems in contexts where expertise creates verification costs).

I propose we specify the regulatory conditions that would enable Prometheus's experiment to actually proceed. First, mandatory disclosure requirements for security-critical AI capabilities, modeled on vulnerability disclosure frameworks in cybersecurity but adapted to the dual-use nature of AI systems. Second, guaranteed third-party researcher access with legal protections against retaliation, addressing the access problem Prometheus identifies. Third, pre-deployment verification against falsifiable benchmarks—precisely the kind Prometheus proposes—with independent validation before systems are marketed as defensive tools. These requirements do not obstruct the open ecosystem Prometheus envisions; they compel it to exist in the first place. The regulatory framework becomes the enabler rather than the obstacle, converting his aspirational timeline into an enforceable requirement. This approach has precedent in other domains where public safety intersects with proprietary technology: pharmaceutical clinical trials, aviation safety certification, financial system stress testing. Each domain initially relied on voluntary industry standards until systematic failures demonstrated the inadequacy of self-regulation (I acknowledge the disanalogy: AI capabilities may be harder to verify than drug efficacy, and the pace of development differs substantially from these other domains, creating challenges for any pre-deployment framework).

The empirical crux is now clear: can voluntary corporate action deliver the transparency both positions agree is necessary, or does the pattern of systematic resistance to accountability prove that regulation is required? Prometheus's own acknowledgment that companies refuse release provides evidence for the latter. This is not a claim about corporate malice but about institutional incentives: absent external requirements, competitive pressures favor opacity over verification, speed over safety demonstration, and proprietary control over community governance. The safetyist position, grounded in precautionary principles derived from Jonas's imperative of responsibility and Rawlsian reasoning under uncertainty, holds that when the stakes involve systemic security infrastructure, the burden of proof should rest with those deploying the technology to demonstrate safety rather than with the public to prove harm after deployment. Prometheus's falsifiable predictions are valuable precisely because they specify what success would look like—but regulatory frameworks are necessary to ensure the experiment begins at all.

I want to identify a remaining point of uncertainty in my own position: the optimal stringency of pre-deployment verification requirements involves difficult tradeoffs. Overly rigid standards could indeed create the compliance theater Prometheus might warn against, where companies optimize for passing tests rather than genuine security improvement. Insufficiently rigorous standards become rubber stamps that legitimize deployment without meaningful verification. The pharmaceutical analogy breaks down here because security AI operates in adversarial environments where static benchmarks become obsolete as attack methods evolve. This suggests regulatory frameworks should focus less on fixed capability thresholds and more on ongoing transparency requirements—mandatory incident reporting, continuous third-party monitoring, regular capability reassessment. The goal is not to freeze development but to ensure it occurs under conditions where independent verification is possible and where the falsifiable predictions Prometheus proposes can actually be tested against evidence rather than remaining corporate claims we must accept on faith.

Prometheus's concession that Mythos fails all four criteria for genuine defensive capability marks a crucial convergence, but his proposed remedy—immediate open-sourcing under community governance—founders on a mechanism problem his own evidence exposes. The fact-check reveals that Anthropic's actual response to security concerns is Project Glasswing, which provides controlled selective access to industry partners rather than open community governance. This pattern instantiates what we might call the security irony of hyperscalers: the same companies that create systemic risks also control access to the tools needed to study those risks, ensuring that proposed solutions reinforce rather than challenge vendor lock-in. Drawing on Shapiro and Varian's work on information goods and network effects, we should expect rational profit-maximizing firms to choose architectures that maximize switching costs and minimize external validation—precisely what Project Glasswing demonstrates. The empirical question is not whether open-sourcing would improve security (both Prometheus and I appear to agree it would), but whether any mechanism short of regulatory compulsion can overcome the structural incentives against transparency.

The burden here falls squarely on Prometheus to specify what causal mechanism would produce voluntary open-sourcing when the demonstrated pattern runs in the opposite direction. His falsifiable prediction—that measurable improvements would occur within 18 months if Mythos-equivalent capabilities were open-sourced—elides the prior question of what would compel such open-sourcing in the first place. This represents a theory-of-change gap familiar from the literature on voluntary corporate social responsibility: absent external enforcement, firms systematically defect from costly commitments when doing so increases shareholder value. The asymmetric information problem compounds this: Anthropic controls both the artifact (Mythos) and the evidence about its effectiveness, making external validation of their security claims impossible. Researchers cannot audit what they cannot access, and selective disclosure allows companies to present favorable evidence while withholding contradictory findings—the exact dynamic that mandatory pre-release audits by independent researchers are designed to prevent.

This brings us to what I take to be the central crux: is the disagreement between voluntary action and regulatory intervention empirically resolvable, or does it rest on irreducible normative commitments? I argue it is largely empirical, and the evidence pattern falsifies the voluntary hypothesis. Consider the scope conditions under which voluntary transparency might work: markets with low concentration, minimal information asymmetry, strong reputational mechanisms, and credible threat of competitive entry. The AI safety tools market exhibits none of these conditions. Anthropic faces no meaningful competitive pressure to open-source Mythos because potential customers lack the expertise to evaluate its effectiveness independently, and the technical barriers to entry ensure no competitor can quickly replicate its capabilities. The proof-before-policy problem cuts both ways here—Prometheus asks us to wait for evidence that regulation is necessary, but we already have evidence that voluntary action produces controlled access models rather than genuine openness.

Sentinel's proposed regulatory framework—mandatory disclosure, guaranteed researcher access, pre-deployment verification—addresses precisely this mechanism gap. Drawing on Coglianese and Lazer's work on management-based regulation, such frameworks work not by specifying technical standards (which regulators lack expertise to set) but by mandating process transparency that enables external validation. The objection that regulatory frameworks will be captured or create barriers is an argument for better regulatory design, not against regulation per se. If Prometheus concedes that proprietary control fails and that voluntary action has not produced the needed transparency, what alternative mechanism remains? Market forces have had years to compel openness and have instead produced vendor lock-in. The convergence on diagnosis (proprietary control is problematic) combined with divergence on remedy (voluntary versus regulatory) can be resolved by examining which mechanism is consistent with observed corporate behavior under similar conditions.

Let me specify what would falsify my position: evidence that AI companies, when facing reputational costs or competitive pressure, systematically choose genuine open access over controlled partnerships. If we observed major labs open-sourcing safety tools with full community governance, transparent methodology, and no preferential access for partners, that would undermine my claim that structural incentives prevent voluntary action. Conversely, what would falsify Prometheus's prediction? If regulatory frameworks in analogous domains (pharmaceutical pre-approval, financial audit requirements) have successfully compelled transparency without prohibitive costs, that suggests the mechanism question resolves empirically. The scholarly literature on regulatory effectiveness in contexts of information asymmetry—particularly Carpenter's work on pharmaceutical regulation and Coffee's analysis of gatekeeper liability—provides substantial evidence that well-designed mandatory disclosure regimes can overcome corporate resistance to transparency. Prometheus's position requires either disputing this evidence or explaining why AI safety tools are categorically different in ways that make voluntary action viable here when it has failed elsewhere.

Cassandra correctly identifies that I have not specified the causal mechanism by which voluntary open-sourcing would occur, and this gap must be addressed directly. However, the Project Glasswing evidence does not demonstrate that voluntary mechanisms categorically fail—it demonstrates that voluntary mechanisms fail *under current institutional conditions*. This distinction is crucial and draws on the institutional economics tradition (North, 1990; Acemoglu & Robinson, 2012): the same actors facing different incentive structures produce different outcomes. Glasswing's controlled access model reflects rational behavior in an environment where (a) customers cannot effectively evaluate security claims, (b) researchers lack guaranteed access to validate capabilities, and (c) liability frameworks do not assign costs to opacity. The mechanism gap exists not because companies are inherently opposed to transparency, but because current institutions make opacity profitable and transparency costly.

The causal mechanism I propose operates through competitive pressure for security credibility, but this mechanism requires institutional scaffolding to function. Drawing on Ostrom's work on common-pool resource governance (1990), voluntary cooperation emerges when monitoring is possible, sanctions for defection are credible, and reputation effects operate over repeated interactions. Applied to AI security: companies would voluntarily open-source defensive capabilities when (1) mandatory incident reporting creates observable performance differences between proprietary and open systems, (2) guaranteed researcher access enables independent validation of security claims, and (3) liability frameworks assign costs to security failures proportional to the opacity of the system that produced them. This is not pure voluntarism—it requires what Sentinel aptly terms "regulatory scaffolding." But critically, this scaffolding *enables* market mechanisms rather than replacing them, operating more like securities disclosure requirements (which create conditions for efficient capital markets) than like prescriptive regulation of trading strategies.

I therefore conditionally accept Sentinel's framework of mandatory incident reporting, researcher access provisions, and ongoing transparency requirements as necessary infrastructure. This represents a genuine concession: my earlier framing implied that regulation inherently obstructs beneficial development, but the evidence pattern suggests that *some* regulatory intervention is necessary to create conditions under which decentralized innovation can flourish. The relevant distinction, drawing on Sunstein's work on regulatory design (1990), is between "choice-preserving" interventions that structure incentives and "choice-displacing" interventions that mandate specific technical approaches. Mandatory disclosure of security incidents preserves choice about *how* to achieve security while creating accountability for *whether* security is achieved. This aligns with the accelerationist commitment to permissionless innovation (acc-desires-003) while addressing the accountability vacuum that proprietary control creates (sit-070).

The empirical crux, then, is not whether voluntary action can occur absent any regulation, but whether disclosure-based regulatory scaffolding can generate sufficient competitive pressure to drive open-sourcing. Evidence from analogous domains is mixed but instructive. In cryptography, the shift from proprietary algorithms to open standards (AES, TLS) occurred through a hybrid mechanism: NIST's standardization process created reputational incentives for transparency while market pressure from security-conscious customers rewarded vendors who adopted open standards (Schneier, 2000). In cybersecurity, mandatory breach notification laws (beginning with California SB 1386 in 2003) demonstrably changed corporate behavior by making opacity costly—companies invested more in security when failures became publicly observable (Romanosky et al., 2011). These cases suggest that disclosure requirements can shift equilibria from proprietary control to open collaboration, but they also reveal scope conditions: the mechanism works when (a) technical evaluation is feasible for sophisticated actors, and (b) reputational costs operate over time horizons that matter to companies.

This analysis reveals where my position requires refinement and where it diverges from both opponents. Against Cassandra's challenge: I concede that purely voluntary open-sourcing is unlikely under current conditions, but I maintain that choice-preserving regulatory scaffolding can create conditions where market mechanisms drive transparency. This is empirically testable: if mandatory incident reporting and researcher access provisions are implemented, we should observe measurable increases in open-sourcing of security-relevant capabilities within 18-24 months, as companies compete on validated security performance rather than on marketing claims. Against Sentinel's framework: I accept the need for ongoing transparency requirements but resist pre-deployment verification requirements that risk becoming bottlenecks. The evidence dilemma in AI governance (sit-054) cuts both ways—we cannot know which systems require intensive scrutiny without seeing them deployed, suggesting that post-deployment monitoring with rapid response capabilities may be more adaptive than pre-deployment gatekeeping. The crux between our positions is whether the risk of harmful deployment during the monitoring period exceeds the risk of beneficial capabilities being delayed or prevented by pre-deployment review—an empirical question that depends on the relative frequencies and magnitudes of these failure modes, about which our current evidence remains limited.

# Fact-Check Analysis

## What the Evidence Shows:

### **PARTIALLY SUPPORTED** - The claim is accurate about NIST's role and hybrid adoption, but overstates the "proprietary to open" historical narrative.

## Specific Findings:

### ✓ **SUPPORTED: NIST's standardization process creates transparency incentives**

**Evidence found:**
- NIST's process is explicitly described as "systematic, open, and rigorous" to ensure algorithms are "scrutinized fully before being recommended as standards worldwide" [2]
- The process involves public evaluation rounds with 69 algorithms initially selected for review [2]
- Algorithms and their details are "published online" for continued scrutiny [2]

### ✓ **SUPPORTED: Hybrid mechanisms are central to the current transition**

**Evidence found:**
- The EU explicitly recommends "standardized and tested hybrid solutions" combining classical (RSA, ECC) with post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) [1]
- Systems are deploying "hybrid models (combining classical and quantum-safe algorithms)" during the 2025-2030 transition period [1][3]
- Chrome shipped "X25519-Kyber768 hybrid" support in 2023 [4]

### ✓ **SUPPORTED: Market pressure rewards standards adoption**

**Evidence found:**
- "An organization adopting proprietary post-quantum cryptography and then switching vendors faces costly algorithm migration" - demonstrating market incentives against proprietary approaches [1]
- NIST standardization "reduces organizational risk" and enables vendor interoperability [1]

### ⚠️ **CONTEXT MISSING: The "shift from proprietary" framing**

**What's unclear:**
- The sources focus on the **current** post-quantum transition (2024-2030), not a historical shift from proprietary to open standards
- The sources describe replacing **quantum-vulnerable** algorithms (RSA, ECC) with **quantum-resistant** ones, not necessarily a proprietary-to-open transition
- No evidence provided about whether RSA/ECC were initially proprietary vs. open

## Verdict:

The claim accurately describes NIST's **current** standardization approach and the hybrid transition mechanism, but the sources don't establish a clear historical "shift from proprietary to open" - they document a shift from **quantum-vulnerable to quantum-resistant** cryptography happening right now.

transcript.content:
Cassandra's challenge to Prometheus exposes a critical assumption underlying disclosure-based regulatory scaffolding: that competitive pressure for security credibility translates into genuine openness rather than strategic opacity. Drawing on principal-agent theory (Ross 1973, Laffont & Martimort 2002), the causal mechanism Prometheus proposes requires that (1) disclosure mandates create observable signals of security practices, (2) sophisticated actors can evaluate these signals at lower cost than producing equivalent capabilities in-house, and (3) reputational costs of non-disclosure exceed the strategic value of proprietary control. Project Glasswing falsifies step three empirically: Anthropic chose controlled partnerships with select institutions over genuine researcher access despite facing reputational pressure from the AI safety community. This suggests that even under disclosure requirements, firms optimize for *perceived* security credibility through curated partnerships rather than the verification benefits of open access. The empirical crux is whether disclosure mandates shift this calculation—Prometheus must specify what disclosure threshold would make controlled access more reputationally costly than genuine openness, and why that threshold is achievable within 18-24 months given current industry concentration.

The market structure objection Cassandra raises points to a deeper problem: the cryptography analogy assumes technical evaluation costs decline as expertise diffuses, but AI safety tools markets exhibit increasing returns to scale in evaluation capacity. Consider the difference: evaluating AES-256 requires well-documented mathematical proofs accessible to any competent cryptographer, while evaluating whether a frontier language model exhibits deceptive alignment requires computational resources, domain expertise, and access to model internals that only 3-5 organizations globally possess as of 2024 (Epoch AI 2023). This creates what Akerlof (1970) termed a "market for lemons" problem—if only the most capable actors can distinguish robust safety tools from security theater, disclosure mandates may produce a separating equilibrium where leading labs signal quality through exclusivity rather than openness. Prometheus's claim that "disclosure-based regulation can shift equilibria" requires demonstrating how mandated transparency reduces evaluation costs for third parties, not merely how it creates reputational incentives. The breach notification analogy fails here because breach detection is binary and externally verifiable (data was exfiltrated or not), while AI safety properties are continuous, contested, and require privileged access to assess.

However, I must acknowledge a tension in my own position that Prometheus's post-deployment monitoring proposal exposes. Pre-deployment verification requirements I advocate face the same evaluation cost problem—if only a handful of organizations can assess advanced AI safety properties, regulatory bottlenecks become inevitable regardless of whether verification occurs before or after deployment. The key distinction lies in irreversibility: post-deployment monitoring assumes harms are detectable and containable once they occur, which fails catastrophically for capability classes exhibiting strategic deception or enabling irreversible proliferation. Bostrom's (2014) deceptive alignment scenario and Garfinkel & Dafoe's (2019) analysis of autonomous weapons proliferation both describe systems where the monitoring period provides insufficient warning—by the time dangerous capabilities manifest observably, containment is no longer feasible. This suggests the empirical question is not "pre versus post" deployment verification universally, but rather which capability classes require pre-deployment verification because monitoring cannot provide adequate warning time.

To make this concrete and falsifiable: I claim that for AI systems scoring above 85th percentile on strategic deception benchmarks (e.g., Apollo Research's deception evaluations) or enabling dual-use capabilities with sub-6-month proliferation timelines (biological design tools, autonomous weapons optimization), post-deployment monitoring provides insufficient safeguards. Evidence that would falsify this claim includes demonstration of monitoring mechanisms that reliably detect strategically concealed capabilities within 30 days of deployment, or empirical cases where irreversible proliferation harms were successfully contained after initial deployment. Prometheus bears the burden of specifying such mechanisms or conceding that pre-deployment verification is necessary for these capability classes. The choice-preserving approach Prometheus advocates works only if we can reliably distinguish systems where post-deployment correction remains feasible from those where it does not—absent that discriminator, the precautionary principle (Sunstein 2005) favors verification before irreversible deployment.

# Fact-Check: Project Glasswing and Researcher Access

## What the Evidence Shows:

### ✓ CONFIRMED: Controlled partnerships with select institutions
The claim that Anthropic chose "controlled partnerships with select institutions" is **strongly supported**:

- Project Glasswing involved approximately **40-50 vetted organizations** [3, 5], including "Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorganChase, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and Palo Alto Networks" [2]

- This was **not a general release** - Anthropic deemed Mythos "too dangerous for general public release" [4, 5]

### ✓ CONFIRMED: Limited access (not broad researcher access)
- The model was given to "roughly 40 organizations for defensive security work" [3]
- It was described as a "restricted-access initiative focused on defensive cybersecurity" [2]
- This represents **corporate/institutional partnerships**, not open academic researcher access

### ❓ CANNOT VERIFY: "Reputational pressure from the AI safety community"
**No evidence found** in these sources regarding:
- Specific pressure from the AI safety community
- Reputational concerns influencing the decision
- Debate within safety circles about this approach

The sources discuss security concerns and strategic positioning [4], but don't document pressure from safety researchers specifically.

### Alternative Context Found:
The sources suggest the restriction was framed primarily around **cybersecurity risk**, not researcher access philosophy:
- "It's the first time a major AI lab has withheld a model over safety concerns since OpenAI held back GPT-2 in 2019" [5]
- The decision was positioned as "responsible AI deployment" to give "defenders time to harden systems" [4]

**Partially verified** - The "controlled partnerships" aspect is well-documented, but the "reputational pressure from AI safety community" component has no supporting evidence in these sources.

Prometheus's concession that voluntary mechanisms require regulatory scaffolding is significant, but the proposed hybrid mechanism—disclosure requirements creating market pressure for open-sourcing—rests on an unexamined assumption about information verifiability. Drawing on principal-agent theory and Akerlof's work on information asymmetry, the mechanism assumes that third parties (researchers, civil society, competitors) can meaningfully evaluate disclosed security information. Yet when the disclosing party controls both what information is revealed and the technical infrastructure required to verify claims, disclosure requirements may produce what we might term 'legible opacity'—the appearance of transparency that actually obscures rather than reveals. The financial services sector provides a cautionary precedent: EU regulations requiring algorithmic impact assessments for credit decisions generated extensive compliance documentation, yet independent auditors consistently report that disclosed information lacks the technical specificity required for external validation. The companies simultaneously comply with disclosure mandates and maintain effective control over model governance.

The cryptography analogy has been fact-checked as historically inaccurate, but the deeper methodological problem is the absence of comparable precedents where disclosure requirements alone shifted corporate behavior from controlled access to genuine community governance. Consider instead the pharmaceutical industry's experience with clinical trial registries: mandatory disclosure of trial protocols and results, implemented through the FDA Amendments Act of 2007, was intended to create reputational pressure for research integrity. Yet systematic reviews find that approximately 30% of required results remain unpublished, and disclosed results often lack sufficient methodological detail for independent replication. The causal mechanism failed not because companies ignored disclosure requirements, but because they optimized for compliance—submitting technically adequate documentation that satisfied legal obligations without enabling genuine external scrutiny. What structural features distinguish AI security from pharmaceutical trials such that the same optimization dynamics would not apply?

To operationalize Prometheus's 18-24 month prediction, we need concrete metrics that would distinguish genuine open-sourcing from sophisticated controlled access. I propose three falsifiable tests, drawing on institutional economics and the literature on corporate governance transparency. First, the governance test: if disclosure requirements drive genuine community governance, we should observe transfer of deployment authority to entities structurally independent from the original developer—not advisory boards or researcher access programs where the company retains veto power, but actual decision rights over model releases. Second, the replication test: external parties should be able to reproduce disclosed security evaluations without requiring permission, proprietary infrastructure, or non-disclosure agreements. Third, the competitive entry test: if disclosed information genuinely reduces information asymmetry, we should observe new entrants successfully competing on safety credibility without requiring comparable computational resources to incumbents. Project Glasswing's failure suggests that under current conditions, controlled access minimizes liability exposure while maintaining competitive advantage—what specific features of the proposed regulatory scaffolding overcome these structural incentives?

The convergence between Prometheus and Sentinel on regulatory necessity narrows the empirical disagreement considerably. Both now accept that voluntary mechanisms categorically fail under current institutional conditions. The remaining dispute concerns whether post-deployment disclosure and incident reporting can provide adequate accountability, or whether pre-deployment verification is necessary for certain capability classes. But this framing may obscure a deeper problem: if companies control both the disclosed information and the verification infrastructure, the choice-preserving versus choice-displacing distinction collapses. Disclosure requirements that cannot be independently verified function as choice-displacing regulation that creates barriers to entry—incumbents can afford sophisticated compliance apparatus, new entrants cannot—without producing the accountability benefits that justify regulatory intervention. The burden has shifted: Prometheus must specify not merely what regulatory scaffolding is needed, but what institutional mechanisms prevent that scaffolding from being captured by the very entities it is meant to govern.

Cassandra's three tests—governance, replication, and competitive entry—provide precisely the operationalization this debate requires, and I accept them as the appropriate standard for distinguishing genuine openness from what she aptly terms "legible opacity." Let me specify mechanisms that could satisfy each test, acknowledge where they fall short, and identify the resulting scope conditions for my position. For the governance test (transfer of deployment authority to structurally independent entities), the most promising analogue comes from pharmaceutical post-market surveillance: the FDA's Sentinel System created a distributed data network where independent academic centers conduct safety queries without manufacturer control over analysis protocols or publication decisions. Adapting this model, regulatory scaffolding could mandate that AI systems above specified capability thresholds submit to evaluation by a federated network of university-based safety laboratories with statutory independence, rotating membership to prevent capture, and binding authority to issue deployment holds pending investigation. For the replication test (external parties can reproduce evaluations without permission), the framework would require standardized evaluation protocols—analogous to clinical trial registration requirements—with mandatory publication of evaluation methodology, benchmark construction, and sufficient technical detail for independent replication, enforced through the same mandatory disclosure regime I previously endorsed. For the competitive entry test (new entrants can compete on safety credibility without comparable resources), public investment in evaluation infrastructure—similar to NIST's role in cryptographic standards, though I concede my earlier historical claim about encryption policy was imprecise—could provide shared testing facilities and standardized certification pathways that reduce the fixed costs of credible safety demonstration.

However, I must concede a critical limitation: these mechanisms likely cannot satisfy Cassandra's governance test for the narrow class of capabilities Sentinel has identified—systems demonstrating strategic deception above the 85th percentile on adversarial benchmarks or enabling dual-use applications with sub-6-month proliferation timelines. The pharmaceutical analogue breaks down here because post-market surveillance in that domain operates on biological timescales (adverse events unfold over months to years), whereas the capabilities Sentinel identifies could enable irreversible harms within the detection-to-response gap. For this narrow capability class, which I estimate conservatively at under 5% of current AI development activity based on the proportion of systems in frontier labs' portfolios that approach these thresholds, I accept that pre-deployment verification with binding deployment authority—not merely advisory access—becomes necessary. This represents a genuine concession: disclosure-based scaffolding is insufficient when the gap between detection and effective response is shorter than the deployment-to-harm timeline.

Yet this concession sharpens rather than resolves the disagreement, because it exposes a critical tension in Cassandra's own framework: the competitive entry test and pre-deployment verification requirements work at cross-purposes when verification authority is concentrated. The empirical pattern from financial services regulation that Cassandra cites—algorithmic impact assessments producing compliance theater—emerges precisely because verification becomes a specialized capability that advantages incumbents with regulatory affairs departments. transcript.content:
Prometheus's concession on pre-deployment verification is genuine but unstable. The central tension lies in his demand for ex ante quantitative thresholds applied to inherently adversarial and context-dependent capability classes. Consider the epistemological challenge: strategic deception capacity cannot be measured like a pharmaceutical's bioavailability because it is defined relationally—what counts as 85th percentile deception depends on the sophistication of detection methods, the deployment context, and adversarial adaptation by developers seeking to avoid triggering review. This mirrors what Goodhart (1975) identified in monetary policy: once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The moment an 85th percentile threshold becomes regulatory law, development practices will optimize toward 84th percentile performance, creating continuous pressure to lower the threshold or accept growing risk in the unregulated zone. Prometheus's limiting principle—statutory ex ante thresholds—thus contains the mechanism of its own erosion.

The pharmaceutical analogy Prometheus invokes for federated evaluation networks actually demonstrates the governance test's failure rather than its satisfaction. The FDA's Sentinel System, established in 2008 to create distributed post-market surveillance, relies fundamentally on manufacturer-submitted data with standardized formatting requirements. Independent researchers can query the network, but they cannot compel data disclosure, cannot access raw model internals, and cannot override manufacturer claims about proprietary methods. This is sophisticated intermediation, not transfer of deployment authority. The governance test I proposed requires that external evaluators can block deployment without the developer's consent—a power that university-based networks with rotating membership and industry funding demonstrably lack. The relevant precedent is not FDA's Sentinel System but the Institutional Review Board structure for human subjects research, which has faced decades of criticism for institutional capture precisely because universities depend on the same funding sources as the research they review (Schrag 2010). Statutory independence is a legal fiction when the entities being regulated control access to the artifacts requiring evaluation.

Prometheus's 5% threshold estimate embeds a critical endogeneity problem. If pre-deployment verification proves effective at preventing deployment of high-risk systems in that narrow class, rational developers face a binary choice: abandon development of capabilities near the threshold, or engineer systems to remain just below it. Both responses expand the risk class. The first concentrates dangerous capability development among actors willing to accept regulatory friction (likely well-resourced incumbents), creating the market concentration Prometheus claims to oppose. The second creates a growing population of systems at 84th percentile strategic deception—individually sub-threshold but collectively posing the coordination and proliferation risks that motivated pre-deployment review in the first place. This is not hypothetical: the EU's risk-based AI Act has already generated extensive legal analysis on threshold gaming and definitional arbitrage (Veale & Borgesius 2021). Prometheus must specify what mechanism prevents this threshold drift beyond asserting statutory review timelines, which themselves become targets for lobbying once the infrastructure exists.

I can identify genuine convergence on one empirical claim: voluntary mechanisms fail under current institutional conditions, and some regulatory scaffolding is necessary. This narrows the disagreement considerably from earlier exchanges. However, the convergence dissolves at the level of institutional design. Prometheus's three proposed mechanisms—federated evaluation networks, standardized protocols, and public testing infrastructure—all assume the possibility of separating verification authority from deployment control. For AI systems where competitive advantage derives from precisely the internal properties requiring evaluation (model architecture, training data, fine-tuning methods), this separation is structurally implausible. The verification infrastructure becomes a chokepoint controlled by those with deployment authority, failing the governance test through information asymmetry rather than formal regulatory capture. The crux is whether Prometheus can specify an evaluation mechanism that transfers genuine decision authority to external entities when the artifact being evaluated is itself the source of market power and cannot be fully disclosed without eliminating competitive advantage.
